limitations: A hosted deployment of the successor is live and serving at the public-alpha Render service with the invitation gate not enforcing, so the running service is reachable without an invitation. It exists for operator verification and carries no qualification evidence: it is not a hosted gate pass, does not change the NO-GO position, and its release tree is whatever was last pushed to the deployment branch rather than a frozen candidate
No live PostgreSQL execution has qualified the successor
No live Render or Neon execution has qualified the successor

Two of the three providers are qualified, on the same candidate. Run 65 on 3 September 2026 passed both live legs: GitHub with seventeen checks and provider evidence for twelve capabilities, GitLab with fourteen checks and nine. The collection reads each listed a real object, fetched it on its own and refused an impossible identifier, because both targets carry permanent fixtures for exactly that purpose; against an unseeded target an empty listing now fails the run rather than passing on reachability alone

GitLab is a proven core path, not feature parity with GitHub. Nine capabilities are Provider-verified -- repository read, branch read and write, recursive tree read, file read, write and delete, and the merge-request and issue reads. Nineteen registry entries are Unavailable for GitLab against four for GitHub: releases, workflows (its pipelines are the analogue and nothing is wired to them), provider rate-limit read, search, stars, LFS, file rename and batch, folder move, live events and access-surface analysis. Dependency audit, recovery and governance are Supported for GitHub and only Experimental for GitLab. Extending it needs no new credential, because GitLab's api scope already covers the missing endpoints -- which is also why its mutation token is broader than GitHub's by construction, confined by the project it can reach rather than by the operations it can perform

The stale-write proof was wrong twice before it was right, and only a live provider said so. It first refused the write in the client, so a provider with no optimistic concurrency would have passed a check named after it. It then sent a synthetic token -- for GitLab, a commit predating the proof file -- which GitHub refused and GitLab accepted, failing runs 63 and 64: GitLab's Files::BaseService#file_has_changed? resolves the path's last commit at both refs and reads 'no commit there' as no information rather than as a conflict, so a token from before the file existed is not stale to it. The proof now replays a real token, sent once while current and required to be accepted, then again after a write has landed under it and required to be refused; run 65 confirmed both halves against gitlab.com and github.com. The local fixture had refused the predating token all along, which is why neither defect was found before a run spent it

All three providers are qualified. Run 68 on 3 September 2026 passed the Gitea leg against gitea.com on first contact -- eleven checks, five capabilities, cleanup verified -- so every Provider-verified claim in the registry now has a live run behind it. The claim had been withdrawn hours earlier on my stated belief that no reachable Gitea instance existed, which was wrong and unchecked: gitea.com is a free public hosted instance and the operator had used it on this project two months before. First contact found no defect, for reasons worth recording rather than mistaking for luck: Gitea keys a conditional update on the file's blob sha exactly as GitHub does and that model was already proven, its contract has no collection probes so there was no fixture surface, and its one real trap -- old_ref_name taking a branch NAME where a commit sha would 404 -- had been found by reading the published specification a day earlier
Manual VoiceOver and desktop screen-reader passes remain required
The browser matrix runs against Playwright route fixtures, so it proves the client contract rather than server route behaviour
An interrupted hosted restore can leave backup or attestation material behind, because that teardown runs on the success path rather than in a finally block

A signed activation envelope is spendable once: its approval identifier is recorded in a CI-side ledger before the run is authorized, and the envelope also pins the dispatch ref so the ledger cannot be evaded by dispatching the same commit on another branch. The ledger is an Actions cache, which a principal holding actions:write can delete; such a principal can already dispatch the workflow, so deletion widens no reach beyond a replay of an identical already-authorized operation
